text: Fine-tuning large language models under strict GPU memory limits requires selecting adaptation methods whose trade-offs match available hardware.

This note analyzes parameter-efficient adaptation, distinguishing architectural designs from empirical measurements across low-rank factorizations, bias tuning, dynamic rank allocation, quantization, and weight decomposition.
We provide a comparative synthesis, isolate an unverified laboratory claim, and specify a controlled single-GPU experimental protocol.
During language model fine-tuning, GPU memory is consumed by weights, gradients, optimizer states, and activations.

In 16-bit fine-tuning with Adam, each parameter requires 2 bytes for the weight, 2 bytes for the gradient, and 8 bytes for momentum buffers, demanding at least 16 bytes per parameter before allocating activations.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning keeps pre-trained weights frozen.
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameterizes the linear update as W = r B A with rank r (d, k).

LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks.
Crucially, researchers must distinguish theoretical parameter savings from measured hardware footprints.
Because frozen weights require no optimizer tracking, Adam memory drops to O(r(d + k)).
Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.
However, this three-fold reduction was measured specifically on a 175B dense model trained with Adam; it cannot be transferred to smaller models or long-context regimens without direct measurement.
Localized bias tuning restricts updates further.
In BitFit, most of the transformer-encoder parameters are frozen, and only the bias terms and the task-specific classification layer are trained.
In BERTBASE and BERTLARGE bias parameters make up 0.09% and 0.08% of the total number of parameters in each model, respectively.
Applying BitFit on pre-trained BERT models is competitive with fine-tuning the entire model.
While BitFit minimizes checkpoint storage, its capacity remains bounded on generation tasks.

Contrasting architectural designs with empirical findings clarifies key tradeoffs, summarized in Table.
Systematic comparison of adaptation methods, explicitly categorizing architectural design specifications versus reported empirical benchmark results.

Method | Precision | Tuned Scope | Zero Latency | Measured Memory Relief | Evaluated Model & Benchmark Finding
Full FT | 16-bit | 100% | Yes | ≥ 16 B/param | Full parameter retraining baseline
BitFit | 16-bit | <0.1% | Yes | Zero weight optimizer states | BERT: matches full FT on GLUE
LoRA | 16-bit | 0.01--1% | Yes | GPT-3: 1.2TB to 350GB | GPT-3: on par with full FT
AdaLoRA | 16-bit | ≤ 1% | Yes | Pruned SVD parameterization | DeBERTaV3: matches full budget
QLoRA | 4-bit (NF4) | 0.1--2% | No | 65B model on 48GB GPU | LLaMA-65B: matches 16-bit FT
DoRA | 16-bit | 0.01--1% | Yes | Magnitude-direction split | LLaMA-7B: +2.8% vs LoRA
QA-LoRA | 4-bit (INT4) | 0.1--1% | Yes | Group-wise 4-bit alignment | LLaMA: on par with QLoRA
A primary trade-off governs weight compression and throughput.
QLoRA compresses static weights 4×, but dequantizing NF4 weights to BF16 per step reduces throughput.
LoRA and DoRA preserve 16-bit throughput and allow zero-latency deployment by folding adapters directly into pre-trained weights.
To evaluate these methods on consumer hardware, we specify a rigorous protocol.

An informal lab assertion recently claimed: ``Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA.'' We treat this statement as explicitly unverified; lacking documented logs, it must not serve as an empirical result or design premise.
Instead, it underscores the need for systematic peak VRAM profiling.
Hardware and Software Stack: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 24GB running Driver 550.54.14, CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.3.0, Transformers 4.40.0, PEFT 0.10.0, bitsandbytes 0.43.0, and FlashAttention-2 (v2.5.8).
Model and Data: Meta-Llama-3-8B in bfloat16, adapted on the Alpaca dataset (52k examples) for 3 epochs (random seed 42).
Evaluated Methods: 16-bit LoRA (r=16, =32), 4-bit QLoRA (NF4, double quantization), 16-bit DoRA (r=16), and 4-bit QA-LoRA (L=32).

Fixed Hyperparameters: Per-device micro-batch size b=1 with gradient accumulation of 16 steps (effective batch 16); AdamW (1=0.9, 2=0.999); learning rate = 2 × 10-4 with linear schedule and 100 warmup steps.
Sequence Tiers: Sequence lengths fixed at 512, 1024, and 2048 tokens; activation checkpointing and FlashAttention-2 enabled globally.

Instrumentation and Harness: Peak VRAM tracked via PyTorch CUDA profiling (max_ _), steady-state throughput in tokens/second (steps 200--500), and downstream zero-shot accuracy on ARC-Challenge and HellaSwag using EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness (v0.4.2).
Several empirical constraints govern this analysis.
Peak GPU memory in parameter-efficient fine-tuning is often dominated by activation memory and sequence length rather than trainable parameter count alone.
Intermediate activations outgrow optimizer buffers at long sequence lengths (L ≥ 2048) unless activation checkpointing is applied.
Reported benchmark gains on specific architectures such as LLaMA or BERT do not guarantee identical memory reductions or downstream accuracy on distinct model families without empirical verification.
